acts.title: Why a joke fails
text: A joke fails for one of four reasons, and only one of them is about the ___ .
The first is that it is ___ — the listener has already worked out where it is going.
The second is translation. A joke built on ___ simply stops existing in another language.
The third is that it may ___ somebody in the room, which is a risk with people you do not know well.
The fourth is subject. Jokes about illness and death make some audiences less ___ and others considerably more so.
What one person finds hilarious, another finds ___ , and neither of them is wrong.

acts.title: Text A · What the survey actually found
text: A few years ago a group of researchers collected more than forty thousand jokes from around the world and asked people to rate them. The finding usually quoted — that different nationalities laugh at different things — is true, provided that you read it carefully.
Respondents from Ireland, the UK, Australia and New Zealand preferred jokes built on wordplay, unless the pun was too obvious, in which case they marked it down hard.
Americans and Canadians rated jokes higher if somebody in them was made to look stupid, as long as it was not the listener.

Several European countries — France, Denmark, Belgium — scored jokes about illness and death well above the average. Even if that sounds grim, the explanation offered is straightforward: joking about a thing makes it less frightening.

items.q: What did the study find?
o: Different countries preferred different kinds of joke

items.q: Why, according to the text, do some countries joke about illness?
o: Joking about a thing makes it less frightening

acts.title: Text B · Why a computer cannot get the joke
text: Almost every joke works the same way. You are led in one direction and the last line sends you somewhere else, and you laugh at the moment you notice you were wrong.

Groucho Marx: “One morning I shot an elephant in my pyjamas. How he got into my pyjamas I’ll never know.” The whole thing turns on which of two readings you had chosen, and you had chosen without noticing.

This is why understanding humour is a reasonable test of intelligence, provided that you define intelligence as speed of re-interpretation rather than knowledge. It also explains why a computer does not laugh — and, more importantly, does not get it. Unless a system holds a great deal of knowledge about the world, it cannot notice that it went the wrong way, because it never went any way at all.
Children have the same trouble until about five. They tell jokes with the shape of a joke and no second reading in them, and they laugh anyway, which is arguably the better system.

items.s: The writer says most jokes lead you in one direction and then redirect you.
The Groucho Marx line depends on two possible readings.
The writer says computers laugh but do not understand.
A system needs world knowledge to notice it went the wrong way.
Children under five tell jokes that work perfectly.

acts.title: Five conjunctions that are not if
rule: All of these attach a condition to a statement, and all of them are translated with the same word in many languages. In English they are not interchangeable: each says something different about how the condition relates to the result.
points: = if not. Never use a second negative with it. Unless you tell me, I won’t know.
= only on this condition. Stronger and more deliberate than if. provided that is the formal one.
= because it might happen. It describes a precaution taken in advance, not a condition.
= this may be true and it changes nothing. A concession, not a condition.
All of these take a present tense for a future meaning, exactly like if: unless it rains, provided that he comes.
eg: Unless you tell me, I won’t know.
= if you do not tell me.
I won’t go unless you come with me.
Never “unless you don’t come”.
You can borrow it as long as you bring it back.
Only on that condition.
I’ll sign, provided that the dates are confirmed.
The same, more formal.
I take an umbrella in case it rains.
A precaution. It may not rain at all.
I’ll take an umbrella if it rains.
A different sentence: I look outside first.
Even if it rains, we’re going.
The rain changes nothing.
Even though it was raining, we went.
even though = although. The rain actually happened.
I don’t tell that joke in case I offend somebody.
Precaution.
Provided that you define intelligence that way, the test works.
Formal condition.
acts.careful: “I’ll take an umbrella in case it rains” and “if it rains” are different. in case means I take it now, before I know. if means I take it only when I see rain.

write.q: Write about 180 words on what is and is not funny where you live — the jokes that travel, the ones that do not, and the rules people follow without stating them. Use unless, as long as or provided that, in case, and even if at least once each, and make the difference between them clear.
write.model:
What people here find funny is almost entirely built on understatement, which is why almost none of it survives translation. Unless you already know the speaker, half the jokes sound like ordinary statements.

What does not travel at all is the wordplay. Russian and Kazakh both allow puns that collapse the moment you explain them, and explaining a pun is the only reliable way to kill it.

The unwritten rule is about who is in the room. Almost any subject is available as long as everybody present has an equal claim to it. The same joke told by an outsider is not the same joke, and everybody knows this without anybody having said it.

My own line is simple enough. I do not tell jokes about somebody’s family in case they have a reason not to laugh, and I do not tell them at all in a work meeting, even if the meeting badly needs one.
